---
title: "Examples of Recent DPOs with Climate Reforms_JA"
---

***Jaffar***: Main takeaways from reading through the Program Documents relevant to the below table:

1)  Most ongoing/active Climate PAs are ***not fiscal*** (e.g., all/almost all of Romania; Philippines; Peru not fiscal)

2)  The **most common** PA relates to increasing **energy efficiency** – typically through a mixture of regulations and/or increasing financing/investment

3)  In the cases of green fiscal measures, they are mainly **about measurement of risk, reporting and transparency**:

    a.  Serbia publishing assessments of fiscal risks from natural disasters;

    b.  Ecuador quantifying contingent liabilities from climate-related disasters in PPP projects;

    c.  Panama has a PA on **climate tagging** of public investment projects

4)  Ecuador has an interesting PA on improving **targeting of fossil fuel subsidies** (reducing coverage)

5)  The strongest **‘green fiscal’ operation is Costa Rica**, which has a few very interesting reforms:

    a.  Reducing tax exemptions to ‘brown’ activities based on a mapping of the climate impact of tax expenditures (to me, this offers a great learning opportunity!)

    b.  Introducing climate considerations into PFM

6)  There is a **concerning** case of Colombia DPL, which rewards the client in one PA for **offering wide-ranging tax exemptions** to encourage renewable energy/green transition. These tax exemptions include being exempt from VAT (which based on tax best practice, we would argue is a tax handle that should not be used to incentivize economic activity) and 50% of income tax (as well as other tax incentives).

7)  Casting our net wider to less recent/ongoing operations (see attached Excel file), there are green fiscal PA related to excises and levies (Fiji; Lao; PNG; Paraguay)

8)  Colombia (2017; 2019; 2023) and Indonesia (2022) are the clearest examples of carbon tax PAs.

Supported reforms include: (1) improving the targeting of fossil fuel subsidies (reducing coverage for large shrimp farmers); (2) issuing a methodology for quantifying contingent liabilities caused by climate-related disasters in PPP projects; (3) reduce import tariffs for lithium batteries needed for renewable energy; (4) mandate all public and semi-public power companies to prepare 5-year energy efficiency plans and monitor implementation of these plans; and (5) fostering the development of a voluntary carbon compensation mechanism by issuing technical guidelines related to the scheme. |

Proposed reforms include: (i) promoting electric mobility (charging stations in the road network; Publicly-procured electric buses); (ii) mainstreaming climate change adaptation and mitigation considerations in PFM and supporting consistent government spending with climate change mitigation and adaptation by appropriately tagging of public investment projects; (iv) strengthening climate resilience and promote a gender responsive blue growth approach to restore and conserve marine-coastal ecosystems by enacting Panama’s Oceans Policy.                                      |
